title: Paulus asks to break out

facts.text: By 22 November 1942 the two arms of the Soviet counteroffensive were closing behind the German Sixth Army at Stalingrad. Before dawn a Soviet tank battalion seized the Don bridge at Kalach.
General Friedrich Paulus, the Sixth Army's commander, flew into the pocket that day and set up his headquarters at Gumrak airfield.
At 7 p.m. he signalled his superiors. His first words were "Army surrounded." He asked for freedom of action if he could not build an all round defence on the open southern flank.
His plan was to pull back XIV Panzer Corps to close the gap in the south and hold a perimeter if supplies could be flown in, and otherwise to give up Stalingrad and break out to the southwest.
His corps commanders backed a breakout. The most outspoken was General Walther von Seydlitz, whose headquarters were only about a hundred yards away.
Hitler was travelling by train from Berchtesgaden back to his headquarters in East Prussia and stopped every few hours to speak by telephone to the Army chief of staff, General Kurt Zeitzler.

At 10.15 p.m. Hitler's answer arrived: "The Sixth Army is temporarily surrounded by Russian forces." The army was to take up a hedgehog defence and await further orders. "I will issue my instructions in good time."
On 23 November the Soviet pincers met at Sovetsky and closed the ring. That night Paulus appealed again for freedom of decision, saying all five of his corps commanders agreed.
On 24 November Hitler decided: the army would hold what he now called Fortress Stalingrad and be supplied by air. Zeitzler had strenuously doubted that it could be done.

Hitler leaned on Hermann Goering's assurance that the Luftwaffe could keep the army supplied. The army needed about 500 tons a day; Luftwaffe transport officers thought 350 tons was the most possible.
Hitler promoted Paulus to field marshal on 30 January 1943; no German field marshal had ever surrendered. Paulus surrendered the next morning.
Of the German soldiers taken prisoner at Stalingrad, only about 6,000 ever came home. Paulus himself later testified for the prosecution at Nuremberg and died in Dresden in 1957.

declassified.fact: Seydlitz did not wait for permission. On the night of 23 November, sure a breakout was coming, he began pulling LI Corps divisions back on the pocket's northeast corner. Hitler, suspecting Paulus, made Seydlitz personally responsible for the whole northern front.

body:
At 7 p.m. General Friedrich Paulus sent two words up the chain: "Army surrounded." The reply took more than three hours.

22 November 1942. Soviet pincers were closing behind the Sixth Army at Stalingrad. Paulus flew into the pocket, set up at Gumrak airfield and asked for freedom of action, which meant a breakout to the southwest if the army could not hold. His corps commanders backed him, Walther von Seydlitz most loudly of all.

At 10.15 p.m. Hitler answered from his train: take up a hedgehog defence and await further orders. Two days later he decided the army would stay and be supplied by air.

Paulus surrendered on 31 January 1943, the morning after Hitler made him a field marshal.
addons: If you were Paulus, would you have broken out without orders?
